title: Mathematics Fundamentals

sources.title: Imperial College London programme specification: H801 MEng Chemical Engineering 2026-27
sources.used_for: module code and title, compulsory status, 10.0 credits (ECTS, 60 per year), Autumn and Spring terms; programme learning outcome on fluency in mathematics; Year 1 assessment mix given only at programme level

about: Mathematics Fundamentals (CENG40007) is a compulsory Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Chemical Engineering, listed with 10 credits (ECTS: the specification gives 60 per year and 240 for the MEng) and running across the Autumn and Spring terms (2026-27 programme specification). Imperial publishes only its title, with no module descriptor, syllabus or module-level assessment breakdown, so the eight topics here are a standard first-year engineering mathematics course chosen by us, not Imperial's own list: calculus, series, complex numbers, linear algebra, ordinary differential equations and partial differentiation, with chemical engineering examples. The programme specification's learning outcomes call for strong fluency in the fundamental principles of mathematics. Check the topics, order and assessment against your lecture list and the department's own module information.
topics: Partial differentiation and functions of several variables

notes.body:
Chemical engineering is full of functions of one variable: concentration against time, vapour pressure against temperature, rate against concentration. You need to handle their limits, derivatives and shapes quickly and reliably.

Functions
- Know the graphs of polynomials, eˣ, ln x, the trigonometric functions and their inverses, and the hyperbolic functions (sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2, cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2).
- Inverse functions: ln is the inverse of exp on (0, ∞), and arcsin has range [−π/2, π/2].
- The Arrhenius form k = A e^(−E/(RT)) becomes linear when you take logs: ln k = ln A − (E/R)(1/T). So a plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with slope −E/R.

Limits
- lim (x → a) f(x) = L means f(x) can be made as close to L as you like by taking x close enough to a (but not equal to it).
- Standard limits: sin x / x → 1 as x → 0; (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e; for any k > 0, xᵏe^(−x) → 0 as x → ∞ (exponentials beat powers).
- L'Hôpital's rule: suppose f and g are differentiable near a (except possibly at a), f(x) → 0 and g(x) → 0 (or both → ±∞), and g′(x) ≠ 0 near a. If lim f′/g′ exists, then lim f/g equals it.
- Example: (1 − cos x)/x² → ½ as x → 0, by applying L'Hôpital twice or using the series cos x = 1 − x²/2 + …

Differentiation
- Rules: product (uv)′ = u′v + uv′; quotient (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²; chain rule (f(g(x)))′ = f′(g(x))g′(x).
- Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x.
- Logarithmic differentiation, for variable powers: if y = xˣ, then ln y = x ln x, so y′/y = ln x + 1 and y′ = xˣ(ln x + 1).
- Standard derivatives: d(arctan x)/dx = 1/(1 + x²); d(ln x)/dx = 1/x; d(aˣ)/dx = aˣ ln a.

Curve sketching and stationary points
- Stationary point: f′(x) = 0.
- Second-derivative test: f″ > 0 gives a local minimum and f″ < 0 a local maximum. If f″ = 0, look at the sign change of f′.
- Point of inflection: f″ changes sign.
- Example: f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1 has f′ = 3(x − 1)(x − 3). There is a local maximum at (1, 5), a local minimum at (3, 1), and an inflection point at (2, 3).
- Also check intercepts, asymptotes, and the behaviour as x → ±∞.

Newton–Raphson (root finding)
xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − f(xₙ)/f′(xₙ). It converges very fast (quadratically) near a simple root if you start close enough, but can fail if f′ is near zero. It is used to solve equations of state and equilibrium relations that have no closed-form solution.

Exam tips: show each rule you apply (chain, product), check that L'Hôpital's conditions hold before using it, and classify every stationary point you find.

Integration turns rates into totals: the amount reacted from a rate, the heat absorbed from a heat capacity, the time to reach a given conversion.

Core techniques
- Standard integrals: ∫ xⁿ dx = x^(n+1)/(n + 1) + c (n ≠ −1); ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c; ∫ eᵃˣ dx = eᵃˣ/a + c; ∫ 1/(x² + a²) dx = (1/a) arctan(x/a) + c.
- Substitution: if u = g(x), then ∫ f(g(x))g′(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du. For definite integrals, change the limits too.
- Integration by parts: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. Choose u to become simpler when differentiated (polynomials, ln x).
  - Example: ∫₀¹ x eˣ dx = [x eˣ]₀¹ − ∫₀¹ eˣ dx = e − (e − 1) = 1.
- Partial fractions for rational functions (if the numerator's degree is not lower than the denominator's, divide first):
  - Distinct linear factors: 1/((x + 1)(x + 2)) = 1/(x + 1) − 1/(x + 2).
  - Repeated factor: A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)².
  - Irreducible quadratic: (Bx + C)/(x² + px + q).
  - Example: ∫₀¹ dx/((x + 1)(x + 2)) = [ln((x + 1)/(x + 2))]₀¹ = ln(2/3) − ln(1/2) = ln(4/3) ≈ 0.288.

Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem
If f is continuous on [a, b] and F′ = f there, then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).

Improper integrals
- Infinite range: ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) dx converges if and only if p > 1 (it equals 1/(p − 1)).
- Integrand blowing up: ∫₀¹ x^(−p) dx converges if and only if p < 1.
- Always write an improper integral as a limit and check that the limit exists.

Applications
- Area between curves: ∫ (upper − lower) dx.
- Mean value of f on [a, b]: (1/(b − a))∫ₐᵇ f dx.
- Volume of revolution about the x-axis: π∫ y² dx.
- Thermodynamics: the enthalpy change on heating is ΔH = ∫ from T₁ to T₂ of C_p(T) dT. For C_p = a + bT this is a(T₂ − T₁) + (b/2)(T₂² − T₁²).
- Reactor design: for a batch reactor with rate r(C), the time to go from C₀ to C is t = ∫ from C to C₀ of dC′/r(C′). This is the same separation of variables you will use for ODEs.

Numerical integration
When there is no antiderivative, or for tabulated data, use the trapezium rule or Simpson's rule. Simpson's rule (an even number of strips, width h) is exact for cubics and has error of order h⁴.

Exam tips: state the substitution or the choice of u and dv, change the limits in definite integrals, and check your answer by differentiating.

Series let you replace awkward functions by polynomials. Engineers use them to linearise models about an operating point, to estimate errors and to evaluate functions numerically.

Sequences and series
- A sequence aₙ converges to L if aₙ gets arbitrarily close to L for all large n.
- A series Σaₙ converges if its partial sums Sₙ = a₁ + … + aₙ converge.
- Necessary condition: if Σaₙ converges, then aₙ → 0. The converse is false: the harmonic series Σ1/n diverges although 1/n → 0.
- Geometric series: Σ (n = 0 to ∞) arⁿ = a/(1 − r) if |r| < 1, and it diverges if |r| ≥ 1.

Convergence tests (for series of positive terms unless stated)
- Comparison: if 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ and Σbₙ converges, then Σaₙ converges.
- p-series: Σ1/nᵖ converges if and only if p > 1.
- Ratio test (any terms): if |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| → ρ, the series converges (absolutely) if ρ < 1 and diverges if ρ > 1. The test says nothing if ρ = 1.
- Example: Σ n/2ⁿ has ratio (n + 1)/(2n) → ½ < 1, so it converges. Its sum is 2. To see this, differentiate Σxⁿ = 1/(1 − x) to get Σ nxⁿ = x/(1 − x)², and put x = ½.

Power series
- Σ cₙ(x − a)ⁿ converges for |x − a| < R and diverges for |x − a| > R, where R is the radius of convergence. Find R with the ratio test. The endpoints must be checked separately.
- Example: Σ xⁿ/3ⁿ is geometric with ratio x/3, so R = 3.

Taylor and Maclaurin series
- If f has derivatives of all orders at a: f(a + h) = f(a) + h f′(a) + h²f″(a)/2! + … + hⁿf⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n! + Rₙ. The series equals f only where the remainder Rₙ → 0.
- Maclaurin series (a = 0) to learn:
  - eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + … (all x)
  - sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − … ; cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − … (all x)
  - ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − … (−1 < x ≤ 1)
  - (1 + x)ᵅ = 1 + αx + α(α − 1)x²/2! + … (|x| < 1; for a non-negative integer α the series stops and holds for all x)
- Example: √1.1 = (1 + 0.1)^(1/2) ≈ 1 + 0.05 − 0.00125 = 1.04875. The true value is 1.048809…, so the error is about 6 × 10⁻⁵, close to the size of the next term (+x³/16 ≈ 6.25 × 10⁻⁵).

Linearisation
- Near an operating point, f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)(x − a). This is how non-linear rate laws and the Arrhenius term are linearised for control and stability analysis.
- For small conversion X, ln(1 − X) ≈ −X, so first-order kinetics look linear at short times.

Exam tips: quote the range of validity of each standard series, find radii with the ratio test, and estimate errors from the first neglected term.

Complex numbers turn up in engineering whenever something oscillates: the characteristic equation of a damped system has complex roots, and e^(iθ) packages a sine and a cosine together.

Forms
- Cartesian: z = x + iy, with i² = −1. Re z = x and Im z = y.
- Conjugate: z̄ = x − iy. z z̄ = |z|² = x² + y².
- Polar: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r e^(iθ), where r = |z| = √(x² + y²) and θ = arg z.
- Take care with the quadrant: arg(−1 + 2i) = π − arctan 2 ≈ 2.034 rad (116.6°), not arctan(−2). The principal argument lies in (−π, π].

Arithmetic
- Add and subtract in Cartesian form.
- Multiply and divide most easily in polar form: moduli multiply and arguments add.
- Division in Cartesian form: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.
- Euler's formula: e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ. So cos θ = (e^(iθ) + e^(−iθ))/2 and sin θ = (e^(iθ) − e^(−iθ))/(2i).

De Moivre's theorem
- (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ for every integer n.
- Uses: powers, such as (1 + i)⁸ = (√2 e^(iπ/4))⁸ = 16 e^(2πi) = 16; and multiple-angle formulae, such as cos 3θ = 4cos³θ − 3cos θ.

Roots
- The equation zⁿ = w (w ≠ 0) has exactly n distinct roots. If w = R e^(iφ), they are R^(1/n) e^(i(φ + 2πk)/n) for k = 0, 1, …, n − 1. They are equally spaced (2π/n apart) on a circle.
- Example: the cube roots of −8 = 8e^(iπ) are 2e^(iπ/3), 2e^(iπ) and 2e^(i5π/3), i.e. 1 + i√3, −2 and 1 − i√3.

Polynomials
- Fundamental theorem of algebra: a polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 with complex coefficients has exactly n complex roots, counted with multiplicity.
- If the coefficients are real, non-real roots come in conjugate pairs.
- Example: z² + 2z + 5 = 0 gives z = (−2 ± √(4 − 20))/2 = −1 ± 2i. Check: the sum of the roots is −2 and their product is 5.

Why this matters for ODEs
For y″ + 2y′ + 5y = 0, trying y = e^(mt) gives m² + 2m + 5 = 0, so m = −1 ± 2i. Then e^((−1+2i)t) = e^(−t)(cos 2t + i sin 2t), and the real solutions are e^(−t)(A cos 2t + B sin 2t): an oscillation that decays.

Loci in the Argand diagram: |z − a| = r is a circle with centre a and radius r. |z − a| = |z − b| is the perpendicular bisector of the segment from a to b.

Exam tips: draw z on an Argand diagram before writing its argument, give all n roots of zⁿ = w, and check the roots of a real polynomial against the sum and product of roots.

Steady-state material balances on several components, or several units, give simultaneous linear equations. Matrices are the natural way to write and solve them.

Vectors (brief)
- a · b = Σaᵢbᵢ = |a||b| cos θ (zero for perpendicular vectors).
- a × b is perpendicular to both a and b, with |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ.
- The equation of a plane with normal n through point a is n · (r − a) = 0.

Matrix algebra
- A (m × n) times B (n × p) gives an m × p matrix. The product is defined only when the inner dimensions agree.
- In general AB ≠ BA, even when both products are defined (they may not even have the same size).
- (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ (for invertible A, B).
- The identity I satisfies AI = IA = A.

Determinants
- 2 × 2: ad − bc.
- 3 × 3: cofactor expansion along any row or column, with signs + − + / − + − / + − +.
- Example: det [[1, 1, 1], [5, 2, 1], [3, 6, 2]] = 1(4 − 6) − 1(10 − 3) + 1(30 − 6) = −2 − 7 + 24 = 15.
- For triangular matrices, det is the product of the diagonal entries.
- A square matrix is invertible if and only if det ≠ 0.

Solving Ax = b
- Gaussian elimination: form [A | b], create zeros below each pivot with row operations, then back-substitute.
- If A is square with det A ≠ 0 there is a unique solution, x = A⁻¹b. In practice you use elimination rather than computing A⁻¹.
- If det A = 0 there are either no solutions or infinitely many: compare rank A with rank [A | b].
- Cramer's rule (xᵢ = det Aᵢ / det A) is fine for 2 × 2 or 3 × 3 by hand, but inefficient for larger systems.

Worked example: a mixing balance
Three feed streams with mass flows x, y, z (kg h⁻¹) are mixed to make 100 kg h⁻¹ of product containing 21% A and 34% B (by mass). The streams contain 50%, 20% and 10% A, and 30%, 60% and 20% B.
- Total: x + y + z = 100.
- A: 0.5x + 0.2y + 0.1z = 21, i.e. 5x + 2y + z = 210.
- B: 0.3x + 0.6y + 0.2z = 34, i.e. 3x + 6y + 2z = 340.
- Elimination: R2 − 5R1 gives −3y − 4z = −290, and R3 − 3R1 gives 3y − z = 40. Adding them: −5z = −250, so z = 50. Then y = 30 and x = 20.
- Check the B balance: 6 + 18 + 10 = 34.
- The determinant of the coefficient matrix is 15 ≠ 0, so this solution is unique.

Degrees of freedom: in process analysis, a balance problem is fully specified when the number of independent equations equals the number of unknowns. In matrix terms, the coefficient matrix is square and has full rank.

Exam tips: scale equations to clear decimals before eliminating, check your solution in an equation you did not use last, and state the determinant or rank to justify uniqueness.

Eigenvalues describe the natural modes of a linear system. In chemical engineering they tell you how quickly coupled tanks or reactors relax to steady state, and whether a steady state is stable.

Definitions
- For a square matrix A, a non-zero vector v with Av = λv is an eigenvector, and λ is its eigenvalue.
- The eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0, a polynomial of degree n.
- For each λ, solve (A − λI)v = 0. The system is singular, so one equation is redundant (for a simple eigenvalue of a 2 × 2 matrix) and v is determined only up to a scalar multiple.
- Checks: Σλᵢ = trace A and Πλᵢ = det A.

Examples
- A = [[1, 2], [2, 1]]: (1 − λ)² − 4 = 0, so λ = 3 with v = (1, 1), and λ = −1 with v = (1, −1).
- A triangular matrix has its diagonal entries as eigenvalues.
- A real matrix can have complex eigenvalues, in conjugate pairs. For example [[0, −1], [1, 0]] (a rotation) has eigenvalues ±i.

Diagonalisation
If A (n × n) has n linearly independent eigenvectors, then A = PDP⁻¹, where the columns of P are the eigenvectors and D is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues. Distinct eigenvalues guarantee this. Real symmetric matrices are always diagonalisable, with real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.

Systems of linear ODEs: x′ = Ax
- If A has n linearly independent eigenvectors vᵢ with eigenvalues λᵢ, the general solution is x(t) = Σ cᵢ e^(λᵢt) vᵢ. The constants come from x(0).
- All eigenvalues with negative real part: every solution decays to 0, so the equilibrium is stable. Any eigenvalue with positive real part: it is unstable.
- At late times the mode whose eigenvalue has the largest real part (the slowest-decaying mode) dominates.

Worked example: two exchanging tanks
Two well-mixed tanks exchange liquid, and each also loses solute to an outlet. The deviations of the concentrations from steady state satisfy x′ = Ax with A = [[−2, 1], [1, −2]] (per hour).
- det(A − λI) = (λ + 2)² − 1 = 0, so λ = −1 or −3.
- λ = −1: v = (1, 1), the two tanks moving together. λ = −3: v = (1, −1), the tanks moving in opposite directions.
- With x(0) = (2, 0): c₁(1, 1) + c₂(1, −1) = (2, 0), so c₁ = c₂ = 1, and x(t) = (e^(−t) + e^(−3t), e^(−t) − e^(−3t)).
- Both modes decay. The (1, −1) mode dies out three times faster, so after a while the tanks have nearly equal deviations, both decaying like e^(−t).

Complex eigenvalues λ = α ± iβ give terms like e^(αt)(cos βt, sin βt): oscillation that decays if α < 0 and grows if α > 0.

Exam tips: check the eigenvalues with the trace and determinant, verify Av = λv for each eigenvector, and interpret the signs of the eigenvalues physically (decay, growth, oscillation).

Unsteady-state balances (accumulation = in − out + generation − consumption) are ODEs. Recognising the type of an equation tells you the method.

First-order equations
- Separable, dy/dx = f(x)g(y): rearrange to ∫ dy/g(y) = ∫ f(x) dx. Check separately for constant solutions where g(y) = 0.
- Linear, dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x): multiply by the integrating factor μ = e^(∫P dx). Then (μy)′ = μQ, so y = (1/μ)(∫ μQ dx + c).
- Use the initial condition to fix the constant.

Chemical engineering examples
- First-order reaction in a batch reactor: dC/dt = −kC gives C = C₀e^(−kt). The half-life is ln 2/k, independent of C₀. For k = 0.1 min⁻¹ it is 6.93 min.
- Second-order reaction: dC/dt = −kC² gives 1/C − 1/C₀ = kt. The time to 90% conversion is 9/(kC₀), which depends on C₀.
- Stirred tank (constant volume V, flow F, inlet concentration C_in): V dC/dt = F(C_in − C). With C(0) = 0 this gives C = C_in(1 − e^(−t/τ)), where τ = V/F is the residence time. For V = 100 L, F = 5 L min⁻¹ and C_in = 2 mol L⁻¹, τ = 20 min, and C reaches 1 mol L⁻¹ at t = 20 ln 2 ≈ 13.9 min.

Second-order linear equations with constant coefficients: ay″ + by′ + cy = f(x)
- General solution = complementary function (CF, solving f = 0) + particular integral (PI).
- CF: try y = e^(mx), which gives the auxiliary equation am² + bm + c = 0.
  - Distinct real roots m₁, m₂: y = Ae^(m₁x) + Be^(m₂x).
  - Repeated root m: y = (A + Bx)e^(mx).
  - Complex roots α ± iβ: y = e^(αx)(A cos βx + B sin βx).
- PI by undetermined coefficients:
  - f a constant or polynomial: try a polynomial of the same degree.
  - f = keᵖˣ: try Ceᵖˣ.
  - f = cos ωx or sin ωx: try C cos ωx + D sin ωx.
  - If the trial function already appears in the CF, multiply it by x (or x² for a repeated root).
- Apply the initial conditions to the full solution (CF + PI), never to the CF alone.

Worked example: y″ + 5y′ + 6y = 12, with y(0) = 0 and y′(0) = 0
- m² + 5m + 6 = 0, so m = −2, −3. CF = Ae^(−2t) + Be^(−3t).
- PI: try a constant: 6y = 12, so y = 2.
- y(0) = 2 + A + B = 0 and y′(0) = −2A − 3B = 0, so A = −6 and B = 4.
- y = 2 − 6e^(−2t) + 4e^(−3t), which tends to the steady state 2.

Systems and higher order: a second-order ODE can be rewritten as two first-order equations, linking this topic to eigenvalues (x′ = Ax) and to numerical methods such as Euler's method, yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + h f(xₙ, yₙ).

Exam tips: classify the equation first, write the auxiliary equation explicitly, and check that the solution satisfies the initial conditions and gives a sensible steady state.

notes.h: Partial differentiation and functions of several variables
notes.body:
Thermodynamic properties depend on several variables at once (P, V, T, composition), so partial derivatives are the everyday language of chemical engineering thermodynamics.

Partial derivatives
- ∂f/∂x is the derivative of f(x, y) with respect to x, holding y constant. In thermodynamics the variable held constant is shown as a subscript, e.g. (∂V/∂T)_P, because it matters which one is fixed.
- Higher derivatives: f_xx, f_yy and the mixed derivatives f_xy and f_yx.
- Symmetry of mixed partials (Schwarz/Clairaut): if f_xy and f_yx exist and are continuous near a point, they are equal there. This is the basis of the Maxwell relations.
- Example: f = x³y² + sin(xy). Then f_x = 3x²y² + y cos(xy) and f_xy = 6x²y + cos(xy) − xy sin(xy).

Total differential and error propagation
- df = f_x dx + f_y dy.
- For a small error estimate, Δf ≈ f_x Δx + f_y Δy. The worst case is |f_x||Δx| + |f_y||Δy|.
- For products and quotients, relative errors add to first order. For the ideal gas law P = nRT/V, ΔP/P ≈ ΔT/T − ΔV/V, so 1% errors in T and V give at most about 2% error in P.

Chain rule
- If f = f(x, y) with x = x(t) and y = y(t), then df/dt = f_x dx/dt + f_y dy/dt.
- For x = x(u, v) and y = y(u, v): ∂f/∂u = f_x x_u + f_y y_u.

Implicit functions and the cyclic relation
- If F(x, y) = 0 defines y as a function of x (with F_y ≠ 0), then dy/dx = −F_x/F_y.
- For three variables linked by F(P, V, T) = 0, with the partial derivatives non-zero: (∂P/∂V)_T (∂V/∂T)_P (∂T/∂P)_V = −1. The partials do not 'cancel' to +1.
- Check with an ideal gas, PV = nRT: (−nRT/V²)(nR/P)(V/(nR)) = −nRT/(PV) = −1.

Stationary points of f(x, y)
- Solve f_x = 0 and f_y = 0 together.
- Classify with D = f_xx f_yy − (f_xy)² (for f with continuous second partial derivatives): D > 0 and f_xx > 0 gives a minimum; D > 0 and f_xx < 0 gives a maximum; D < 0 gives a saddle; D = 0 is inconclusive.
- Example: f = x² + xy + y² − 3x. The equations 2x + y = 3 and x + 2y = 0 give (2, −1). D = 4 − 1 = 3 > 0 and f_xx = 2 > 0, so it is a minimum, with f = −3.

Least squares (application)
To fit y = mx + c to data, minimise S(m, c) = Σ(yᵢ − mxᵢ − c)². Setting ∂S/∂m = ∂S/∂c = 0 gives the normal equations. This is how kinetic parameters are fitted, for example from an Arrhenius plot.

Exam tips: say which variables are held constant, check mixed partials agree as a test of your algebra, and use the cyclic relation to obtain derivatives that are hard to measure from ones that are easy.

When A is m × n and B is n × p; the product is m × p.
No. Matrix multiplication is not commutative.
B⁻¹A⁻¹ (order reversed), for invertible A and B.
Ax = b has exactly one solution for every b.
Ax = b has either no solution or infinitely many; compare rank A with rank [A | b].
xᵢ = det Aᵢ / det A, where Aᵢ is A with column i replaced by b; needs det A ≠ 0.
The product of its diagonal entries.
Av = λv with v ≠ 0; the eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0.

cards.f: General solution of x′ = Ax (n independent eigenvectors)
cards.b: x(t) = Σ cᵢ e^(λᵢt) vᵢ, with the cᵢ fixed by x(0).
Stable (all solutions → 0) if every eigenvalue has negative real part; unstable if any has positive real part.

cards.f: Which mode dominates at late times?
cards.b: The one whose eigenvalue has the largest real part (the slowest-decaying mode).
Give oscillations e^(αt)cos βt and e^(αt)sin βt; they decay if α < 0.
Real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors, always diagonalisable.
±i: a real matrix can have complex eigenvalues.

cards.f: Integrating factor for y′ + P(x)y = Q(x)
cards.b: μ = e^(∫P dx); then (μy)′ = μQ.
t½ = ln 2/k, independent of the initial concentration.
1/C − 1/C₀ = kt; the time to 90% conversion is 9/(kC₀).
C = C_in(1 − e^(−t/τ)), with residence time τ = V/F.

cards.f: Auxiliary equation with a repeated root m
cards.b: y = (A + Bx)e^(mx).

cards.f: Auxiliary equation with complex roots α ± iβ
cards.b: y = e^(αx)(A cos βx + B sin βx).

cards.f: Trial PI when the trial function is already in the CF
cards.b: Multiply the trial function by x (by x² if it matches a repeated root).

cards.f: When do you apply initial conditions?
cards.b: To the full solution, CF + PI, after finding the PI.
If f_xy and f_yx exist and are continuous near a point, then f_xy = f_yx there.
df = f_x dx + f_y dy.
(∂P/∂V)_T (∂V/∂T)_P (∂T/∂P)_V = −1, for F(P, V, T) = 0 with non-zero partials.
dy/dx = −F_x/F_y (where F_y ≠ 0).
ΔP/P ≈ ΔT/T − ΔV/V; the worst case is the sum of the magnitudes.

cards.f: Stationary point of f = x² + xy + y² − 3x
cards.b: (2, −1), a minimum with f = −3 (D = 3 > 0, f_xx = 2 > 0).

cards.f: Normal equations for a straight-line fit
cards.b: Set ∂S/∂m = 0 and ∂S/∂c = 0, where S = Σ(yᵢ − mxᵢ − c)².
It records which variable is held constant; the value depends on that choice.

questions.q: What is d/dx (xˣ) for x > 0?
questions.why: Write y = xˣ, so ln y = x ln x. Differentiating, y′/y = ln x + 1, so y′ = xˣ(ln x + 1). x · x^(x−1) treats the exponent as a constant (power rule), but the exponent varies. xˣ ln x treats the base as a constant (exponential rule), but the base varies too. ln x + 1 is y′/y: it forgets to multiply back by y after differentiating ln y.

questions.q: What is lim (x → 0) of (1 − cos x)/x²?
questions.why: cos x = 1 − x²/2 + x⁴/24 − …, so (1 − cos x)/x² = ½ − x²/24 + … → ½ (or apply L'Hôpital twice: sin x/(2x) → ½). 0 assumes that because the numerator tends to 0 the limit is 0, ignoring that the denominator also tends to 0. 1 confuses this with the standard limit sin x / x → 1. 2 inverts the Taylor coefficient, dividing x² by x²/2 instead of the other way round.

questions.q: Find and classify the stationary points of f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1, and locate its point of inflection.
markScheme: Stationary points at x = 1 and x = 3
f″ = 0 at x = 2 and changes sign there: inflection at (2, 3)
questions.modelAnswer: f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3), which is zero at x = 1 and x = 3. f″(x) = 6x − 12. At x = 1, f″ = −6 < 0, so there is a local maximum with f(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 + 1 = 5. At x = 3, f″ = 6 > 0, so there is a local minimum with f(3) = 27 − 54 + 27 + 1 = 1. f″ = 0 at x = 2 and changes sign from negative to positive there, so (2, f(2)) = (2, 3) is a point of inflection.

questions.q: What is ∫₀¹ x eˣ dx?
questions.why: By parts with u = x, dv = eˣ dx: [x eˣ]₀¹ − ∫₀¹ eˣ dx = e − (e − 1) = 1. e is just the boundary term [x eˣ]₀¹, forgetting to subtract ∫ v du. 2e − 1 adds ∫ v du instead of subtracting it. e/2 comes from multiplying the antiderivatives of the two factors, (x²/2)eˣ, and evaluating from 0 to 1; there is no such product rule for integrals.

questions.q: Which of these improper integrals converges?
questions.why: ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) dx converges only when p > 1; with p = 2 it equals 1. With p = 1 the integral is ln x, which grows without bound. With p = ½ it is 2√x, which also diverges; it would need p > 1, not just p > 0. ∫₀¹ x⁻² dx diverges at the lower limit because near 0 you need p < 1: applying the 'p > 1' test from the infinite-range case to a singularity at 0 gets the condition backwards.

questions.q: Use partial fractions to evaluate ∫₀¹ dx/((x + 1)(x + 2)).
questions.modelAnswer: Write 1/((x + 1)(x + 2)) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 2). Then 1 = A(x + 2) + B(x + 1); x = −1 gives A = 1 and x = −2 gives B = −1. So the integral is [ln(x + 1) − ln(x + 2)]₀¹ = [ln((x + 1)/(x + 2))]₀¹ = ln(2/3) − ln(1/2) = ln(4/3) ≈ 0.288.

questions.q: What is the Maclaurin series of ln(1 + x) up to the x³ term?
questions.why: The derivatives of ln(1 + x) at 0 are 1, −1, 2, so the coefficients are 1, −1/2, 2/6 = 1/3: x − x²/2 + x³/3. x + x²/2 + x³/3 drops the alternating signs; it is the series of −ln(1 − x). x − x²/2! + x³/3! uses factorials as in eˣ, but the factorials cancel against the derivatives (n − 1)!, leaving 1/n. 1 + x − x²/2 adds a constant 1, but ln(1) = 0.

questions.q: What is the radius of convergence of Σ (n = 0 to ∞) xⁿ/3ⁿ?
questions.why: The series is geometric with ratio x/3, so it converges when |x/3| < 1, i.e. R = 3 (the ratio test gives the same). 1/3 inverts the ratio-test condition. 1 assumes every power series has radius 1, as Σxⁿ does, but dividing each term by 3ⁿ widens the interval of convergence. ∞ wrongly assumes a geometric series always converges, but it needs |ratio| < 1.

questions.q: (a) Use the ratio test to show that Σ (n = 1 to ∞) n/2ⁿ converges. (b) By differentiating the geometric series, find its sum.
markScheme: Σ (n ≥ 0) xⁿ = 1/(1 − x) for |x| < 1; differentiate: Σ nx^(n−1) = 1/(1 − x)²
Multiply by x: Σ nxⁿ = x/(1 − x)²
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) aₙ = n/2ⁿ, so aₙ₊₁/aₙ = (n + 1)/(2n) → ½ < 1. By the ratio test the series converges.
(b) For |x| < 1, Σ (n ≥ 0) xⁿ = 1/(1 − x). A power series can be differentiated term by term inside its radius of convergence, giving Σ (n ≥ 1) nx^(n−1) = 1/(1 − x)². Multiplying by x gives Σ nxⁿ = x/(1 − x)². At x = ½ this is (½)/(½)² = 2.

questions.q: What is (1 + i)⁸?
questions.why: 1 + i = √2 e^(iπ/4), so (1 + i)⁸ = (√2)⁸ e^(i2π) = 16. 256 takes |1 + i| as 2 instead of √2. 2 raises each term separately (1⁸ + i⁸), ignoring all the cross terms of the binomial expansion. 8√2 multiplies the modulus by 8 instead of raising it to the 8th power.

questions.q: Which set gives all the solutions of z³ = −8?
questions.why: −8 = 8e^(iπ), so z = 2e^(i(π + 2πk)/3) for k = 0, 1, 2, giving 1 + i√3, −2 and 1 − i√3. '−2 only' gives just the real root, but a cubic has three complex roots. 2, −1 ± i√3 are the cube roots of +8 (argument 0 instead of π). −2, ±2i come from mis-factorising z³ + 8 as (z + 2)(z² + 4); the correct factorisation is (z + 2)(z² − 2z + 4), and indeed (2i)³ = −8i, not −8.

questions.q: Solve z² + 2z + 5 = 0. Express the roots in polar form (modulus and argument in radians), and check your answers using the sum and product of the roots.
questions.modelAnswer: By the quadratic formula, z = (−2 ± √(4 − 20))/2 = (−2 ± 4i)/2 = −1 ± 2i. Each root has modulus √(1 + 4) = √5. −1 + 2i is in the second quadrant, so its argument is π − arctan 2 ≈ 2.034 rad. Its conjugate has argument ≈ −2.034 rad. So z = √5 e^(±2.034i). Check: the sum of the roots is −2 = −b/a, and the product is (−1)² + 2² = 5 = c/a.

questions.why: Expanding along the first row with signs + − +: 1(2·2 − 1·6) − 1(5·2 − 1·3) + 1(5·6 − 2·3) = −2 − 7 + 24 = 15. 29 adds all three cofactor terms, ignoring the minus sign on the middle one (−2 + 7 + 24). −15 uses the sign pattern − + − along the first row, which flips the sign of the answer. 4 multiplies the diagonal entries, which gives the determinant only for a triangular matrix.

questions.q: A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 2. Which statement is true?
options: AB = BA, because both products exist
questions.why: (2 × 3)(3 × 2) gives a 2 × 2 matrix, and (3 × 2)(2 × 3) gives a 3 × 3 matrix; each product takes the outer dimensions. Saying both are 2 × 2 takes the size of AB for both. BA is defined too, because B has 2 columns and A has 2 rows. The two products cannot be equal: they are not even the same size, and matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.

questions.q: Three feed streams with flows x, y, z kg h⁻¹ are mixed to produce 100 kg h⁻¹ containing 21% A and 34% B. The streams contain 50%, 20% and 10% A, and 30%, 60% and 20% B, respectively. Set up the balances and solve by Gaussian elimination.
questions.modelAnswer: Total: x + y + z = 100. A balance: 0.5x + 0.2y + 0.1z = 0.21 × 100 = 21, or 5x + 2y + z = 210. B balance: 0.3x + 0.6y + 0.2z = 34, or 3x + 6y + 2z = 340. Eliminate x: (R2 − 5R1) gives −3y − 4z = −290, and (R3 − 3R1) gives 3y − z = 40. Adding these: −5z = −250, so z = 50. Then 3y = 40 + 50 = 90, so y = 30, and x = 100 − 30 − 50 = 20. Check: 6 + 18 + 10 = 34 kg h⁻¹ of B. The coefficient determinant is 15 ≠ 0, so the solution is unique.

questions.q: What are the eigenvalues of [[1, 2], [2, 1]]?
questions.why: det(A − λI) = (1 − λ)² − 4 = 0 gives 1 − λ = ±2, so λ = −1 or 3 (sum 2 = trace, product −3 = det). 1 and 1 are the diagonal entries, which are eigenvalues only for triangular matrices. 2 and −2 come from taking ± the off-diagonal entry. −3 and 1 have the right sizes but the signs are flipped, from writing the characteristic equation as (1 + λ)² − 4 = 0 (i.e. using A + λI instead of A − λI), which gives λ + 1 = ±2.

questions.q: A linear system x′ = Ax has eigenvalues −1 and −3, with eigenvectors v₁ and v₂. What happens to a typical solution as t → ∞?
options: It decays to 0, approaching 0 along the direction of v₁
It decays to 0, approaching 0 along the direction of v₂
It oscillates, because there are two eigenvalues
questions.why: x = c₁e^(−t)v₁ + c₂e^(−3t)v₂, and both terms decay. The e^(−3t) term dies faster, so the solution approaches 0 along v₁, the slow mode. Approaching along v₂ picks the fast mode, which is the first to vanish. Growth needs an eigenvalue with positive real part, and both here are negative. Oscillation needs complex eigenvalues; two real eigenvalues give no oscillation however many there are.

questions.q: Solve x′ = Ax with A = [[−2, 1], [1, −2]] and x(0) = (2, 0). Describe the behaviour as t → ∞.
markScheme: Eigenvectors: (1, 1) for λ = −1 and (1, −1) for λ = −3
Initial condition: c₁ = c₂ = 1, so x = (e^(−t) + e^(−3t), e^(−t) − e^(−3t))
Both components → 0; the e^(−t) mode dominates, so the components become nearly equal
questions.modelAnswer: det(A − λI) = (−2 − λ)² − 1 = 0 gives λ + 2 = ±1, so λ = −1 or −3. For λ = −1, (A + I)v = 0 gives −v₁ + v₂ = 0, so v = (1, 1). For λ = −3, (A + 3I)v = 0 gives v₁ + v₂ = 0, so v = (1, −1). The general solution is x = c₁e^(−t)(1, 1) + c₂e^(−3t)(1, −1). At t = 0, c₁ + c₂ = 2 and c₁ − c₂ = 0, so c₁ = c₂ = 1. So x₁ = e^(−t) + e^(−3t) and x₂ = e^(−t) − e^(−3t). Both decay to 0 (stable, since both eigenvalues are negative). The e^(−3t) part dies out first, so for large t, x₁ ≈ x₂ ≈ e^(−t).

questions.q: A first-order reaction has k = 0.1 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
questions.why: C = C₀e^(−kt) halves when kt = ln 2, so t½ = ln 2/0.1 ≈ 6.93 min. 10 min is 1/k, the time constant, at which C has fallen to 1/e ≈ 37%, not 50%. 5 min is 1/(2k), the time to halve if the concentration kept falling in a straight line at its initial rate kC₀. 0.0693 min multiplies k by ln 2 instead of dividing.

questions.q: What is the general solution of y″ + 4y′ + 4y = 0?
questions.why: The auxiliary equation m² + 4m + 4 = (m + 2)² = 0 has the repeated root m = −2, so y = (A + Bt)e^(−2t). Ae^(−2t) + Be^(−2t) is really just one arbitrary constant times e^(−2t); a second-order equation needs two independent solutions, hence the factor t. (A + Bt)e^(2t) has the sign of the root wrong. A cos 2t + B sin 2t treats the roots as ±2i, which would be the solution of y″ + 4y = 0.

questions.q: A stirred tank of constant volume 100 L is fed at 5 L min⁻¹ with a solution of concentration 2 mol L⁻¹, and the outlet flow is also 5 L min⁻¹. Initially the tank contains pure water. (a) Write a balance for the concentration C(t) and solve it. (b) When does C reach 1 mol L⁻¹?
markScheme: dC/dt = (2 − C)/20, separable or linear, τ = 20 min
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Solute balance: V dC/dt = F C_in − F C, so 100 dC/dt = 10 − 5C, i.e. dC/dt = (2 − C)/20. Separating: ∫ dC/(2 − C) = ∫ dt/20, so −ln(2 − C) = t/20 + k. With C(0) = 0, this gives 2 − C = 2e^(−t/20) and C = 2(1 − e^(−t/20)) mol L⁻¹. It approaches the inlet value 2 with time constant τ = V/F = 20 min.
(b) C = 1 when e^(−t/20) = ½, i.e. t = 20 ln 2 ≈ 13.9 min.

questions.q: For any equation of state F(P, V, T) = 0 with non-zero partial derivatives, what is (∂P/∂V)_T (∂V/∂T)_P (∂T/∂P)_V?
options: It depends on the equation of state
questions.why: The cyclic relation gives −1 for any such relation, as the ideal gas check (−nRT/V²)(nR/P)(V/(nR)) = −1 confirms. 1 comes from treating the partial derivatives as fractions that cancel, which ignores that a different variable is held constant in each. 0 confuses the result with dF = 0: differentiating the constraint gives F_P dP + F_V dV + F_T dT = 0, but the product of the three partials is (−F_V/F_P)(−F_T/F_V)(−F_P/F_T) = −1, and none of the factors is zero. The value does not depend on the equation of state, because it follows from the implicit function rule for any F with non-zero partials.

questions.q: f(x, y) = x³y² + sin(xy). What is ∂²f/∂y∂x?
questions.why: f_x = 3x²y² + y cos(xy). Differentiating with respect to y, using the product rule on y cos(xy): 6x²y + cos(xy) − xy sin(xy). 6x²y + cos(xy) forgets that cos(xy) also depends on y, so it misses the product-rule term. 6x²y − xy sin(xy) differentiates only the cosine and forgets the derivative of the factor y. 6x²y + cos(xy) + xy sin(xy) uses d(cos u) = +sin u du, the wrong sign.

questions.q: Find and classify the stationary point of f(x, y) = x² + xy + y² − 3x.
questions.modelAnswer: f_x = 2x + y − 3 and f_y = x + 2y. Setting both to zero: from the second, x = −2y. Substituting, −4y + y = 3, so y = −1 and x = 2. Second derivatives: f_xx = 2, f_yy = 2, f_xy = 1, so D = 2 × 2 − 1² = 3 > 0. With f_xx > 0, (2, −1) is a local minimum (in fact the global minimum, since f is a positive-definite quadratic plus a linear term). The minimum value is f(2, −1) = 4 − 2 + 1 − 6 = −3.

questions.q:
In a batch reactor the consecutive first-order reactions A → B → C occur with rate constants k₁ and k₂ (k₁ ≠ k₂). Initially [A] = A₀ and [B] = [C] = 0.
(a) Write down ODEs for a(t) = [A] and b(t) = [B], and solve for a(t). [3]
(b) Solve the linear ODE for b(t) using an integrating factor. [7]
(c) Show that b(t) is greatest at t_max = ln(k₂/k₁)/(k₂ − k₁). [5]
(d) For k₁ = 1 h⁻¹ and k₂ = 2 h⁻¹, find t_max and the maximum concentration of B as a fraction of A₀. [5]
markScheme: (a) da/dt = −k₁a, db/dt = k₁a − k₂b; a = A₀e^(−k₁t)
(b) b′ + k₂b = k₁A₀e^(−k₁t); integrating factor e^(k₂t)
(c) b′ = 0 gives k₁e^(−k₁t) = k₂e^(−k₂t), so t_max = ln(k₂/k₁)/(k₂ − k₁); it is a maximum since b rises from 0 and tends to 0
(d) b_max = A₀(e^(−ln 2) − e^(−2 ln 2)) = A₀(½ − ¼) = A₀/4
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A is consumed at rate k₁a, and B is formed at rate k₁a and consumed at rate k₂b. So da/dt = −k₁a and db/dt = k₁a − k₂b. The first is separable: a(t) = A₀e^(−k₁t).

(b) Substituting, db/dt + k₂b = k₁A₀e^(−k₁t). This is linear with P = k₂, so the integrating factor is e^(k₂t), and d/dt(b e^(k₂t)) = k₁A₀e^((k₂−k₁)t). Integrating (k₁ ≠ k₂): b e^(k₂t) = k₁A₀e^((k₂−k₁)t)/(k₂ − k₁) + c. At t = 0, b = 0, so c = −k₁A₀/(k₂ − k₁). Hence b(t) = [k₁A₀/(k₂ − k₁)](e^(−k₁t) − e^(−k₂t)).

(c) db/dt = [k₁A₀/(k₂ − k₁)](−k₁e^(−k₁t) + k₂e^(−k₂t)) = 0 when k₂e^(−k₂t) = k₁e^(−k₁t), i.e. e^((k₂−k₁)t) = k₂/k₁, so t_max = ln(k₂/k₁)/(k₂ − k₁). This is the only stationary point for t > 0. Since b(0) = 0, b > 0 for t > 0 (the bracket has the same sign as k₂ − k₁), and b → 0 as t → ∞, it must be a maximum.

(d) With k₁ = 1 and k₂ = 2: t_max = ln 2/1 ≈ 0.693 h (about 42 minutes). b(t) = A₀(e^(−t) − e^(−2t)), so b_max = A₀(½ − ¼) = A₀/4. At most a quarter of the A fed is present as B at any time, which matters if B is the desired product and the reactor must be stopped at the right moment.

questions.q:
A damped system is described by y″ + 2y′ + 5y = 10 cos t, with y(0) = 0 and y′(0) = 0.
(a) Find the complementary function, using complex roots of the auxiliary equation. [4]
(b) Find a particular integral of the form a cos t + b sin t. [5]
(c) Apply the initial conditions to obtain y(t). [6]
(d) Describe the behaviour for large t, and write the steady-state response as R cos(t − φ), giving R and φ. [5]
markScheme: (a) m² + 2m + 5 = 0, so m = −1 ± 2i; CF = e^(−t)(A cos 2t + B sin 2t)
(b) Substitution gives (4a + 2b) cos t + (4b − 2a) sin t = 10 cos t
(b) 4a + 2b = 10 and 4b − 2a = 0, so a = 2, b = 1: PI = 2 cos t + sin t
(d) The transient decays like e^(−t), leaving 2 cos t + sin t
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Auxiliary equation m² + 2m + 5 = 0, so m = (−2 ± √(4 − 20))/2 = −1 ± 2i. The CF is e^(−t)(A cos 2t + B sin 2t).

(b) Try y_p = a cos t + b sin t. Then y_p′ = −a sin t + b cos t and y_p″ = −a cos t − b sin t. Substituting: cos t terms: −a + 2b + 5a = 4a + 2b; sin t terms: −b − 2a + 5b = 4b − 2a. Matching with 10 cos t: 4a + 2b = 10 and 4b − 2a = 0. So a = 2b, 10b = 10, b = 1 and a = 2. y_p = 2 cos t + sin t. (The trial is valid because cos t and sin t are not in the CF.)

(c) y = e^(−t)(A cos 2t + B sin 2t) + 2 cos t + sin t. y(0) = A + 2 = 0, so A = −2. Differentiating: y′ = e^(−t)[(−A + 2B) cos 2t + (−B − 2A) sin 2t] − 2 sin t + cos t, so y′(0) = −A + 2B + 1 = 2 + 2B + 1 = 0, giving B = −3/2. Therefore y(t) = −e^(−t)(2 cos 2t + (3/2) sin 2t) + 2 cos t + sin t.

(d) The CF part is a transient: it oscillates at angular frequency 2 inside an envelope e^(−t), and after a few time units it is negligible. What remains is the steady-state response 2 cos t + sin t at the forcing frequency. Writing it as R cos(t − φ) = R cos φ cos t + R sin φ sin t gives R cos φ = 2 and R sin φ = 1, so R = √5 ≈ 2.24 and φ = arctan(1/2) ≈ 0.464 rad (26.6°). The response lags the forcing by about 26.6°.
